strengths: The core idea of coupling a frozen closed-source LLM with a lightweight trainable model in an evolutionary loop, where experience is internalized via parameter updates rather than static prompting or RAG, is a sensible and reasonably novel direction for LLM-driven discrete optimization.

Section 4.2 provides a candid empirical narrative on why SFT and naive RL fail in this setting (catastrophic forgetting; reward-induced collapse), and the similarity-based DPO data synthesis (Section 4.3, Algorithm 2) is a concrete, well-specified mechanism that plausibly stabilizes preference learning.

Results are reported as mean ± std over 10 runs, with multiple evaluation metrics (HV, uniqueness, diversity, validity), and the paper includes dedicated ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements.
The appendix adds useful implementation detail (fixed reference model for DPO, full pair-construction pseudocode, prompt templates, additional co-evolutionary curves).
weaknesses: The central 'state-of-the-art' claim is not supported against actual prior SOTA. Table 1 compares only single-model baselines (Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4o) and the authors' own SFT/RL variants; no numbers from ExLLM or MoLLEO—the two benchmarks the paper builds on—are reported. Without these comparisons, 'SOTA Pareto front quality' is unsubstantiated.

Statistical support is weak given the noise: e.g., dpo_coevolve HV is 0.847±0.138 vs rl_coevolve 0.709±0.219 and sft_coevolve 0.709±0.288—overlapping distributions with no significance tests. Also, dpo_coevolve:api (0.855) barely differs from dpo_coevolve (0.847), undercutting the claim that co-evolution 'enhances the capabilities of both models'; a frozen API model cannot meaningfully improve, so the framing of 'mutual inspiration' is overstated.

Generality claims are not evidenced: the framework is claimed 'unified and general-purpose,' yet it is evaluated on exactly one task (five-objective molecular design), one local model (Qwen2.5-7B), and one prompt template. No second domain or second local model is tested.

The DPO preference pairs are constructed by scalarizing a multi-objective score, which conflicts with the stated multi-objective Pareto framing; how the scalarization/ranking is defined is never specified, making the central training signal underspecified.

The similarity-based data synthesis is motivated as the key stabilizer, but there is no ablation isolating its contribution versus plain DPO pairs—the evidence is limited to qualitative loss-curve descriptions (Figure 4).

Notable inconsistencies and sloppiness: GFlowNets are introduced in Section 3.3 and mentioned in the appendix sweeps but never used or compared; the appendix prompt asks to 'decrease the DRD2 value' (typically DRD2 activity is maximized in these benchmarks) and contains errors ('GSK303b2', 'SIMLES', 'ZINK'); Figure 3's 'co-evolutionary curve' plots only the two single models and does not visibly include the MCCE trajectory it purports to illustrate; the claimed validity advantage of MCCE does not hold (0.820 vs 0.905 for sft_coevolve).

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: key hyperparameters (β, update frequency f, L, r, actual values used for the similarity windows) are described qualitatively but not reported numerically, and no code link or artifact is verifiable from the manuscript itself.
There is no limitations section; trade-offs such as the drop in uniqueness (0.660 vs 0.702 for GPT-4o) and validity under DPO training are presented without discussion.

strengths: The core idea—pairing a frozen closed-source LLM with a lightweight trainable local model and periodically refining the local model from 'breakthrough' search trajectories via DPO—is a sensible and timely direction for LLM-driven evolutionary optimization.

The paper includes an honest empirical comparison of alternative training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO) within the same evolutionary loop, and provides qualitative analyses (loss curves, output distribution shifts, co-evolutionary trajectories) that illuminate why DPO works better in this setting (catastrophic forgetting for SFT, instability for RL).

The similarity-based DPO pair construction with stratified fallback rules (Section 4.3, Algorithms 1-2) is a concrete, well-specified engineering contribution aimed at stabilizing preference training under distribution shift, and results are reported as mean ± std over 10 runs.
The manuscript addresses ethics, LLM-usage, and reproducibility with dedicated statements, and key algorithmic details are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'state-of-the-art Pareto front quality' is not supported by the evidence: Table 1 compares only the authors' own variants (single models, and their SFT/RL/DPO ablations). No external baselines from the literature—e.g., MoLLEO (Wang et al., 2024) and ExLLM (Ran et al., 2025), which the paper itself cites as the motivating benchmarks—are actually run or compared against, so the SOTA claim is unsupported.

The 'co-evolution' framing is overstated and potentially misleading. The frozen API LLM never updates its parameters, so it cannot 'evolve' or 'grow by learning from shared experience' as claimed. The claimed 'mutual inspiration benefits both models' is not substantiated: any apparent improvement of the API model's outputs is a function of population/prompt changes, not learning, and the paper provides no mechanism-level analysis of what the frozen model gains.

Generality claims are untested. The paper claims a 'unified and general-purpose optimization framework' applicable beyond drug discovery, but evaluates on a single domain (five-objective molecular design on ZINC) with a single local model (Qwen2.5-7B) and two specific API models. There is no evidence on any other discrete optimization task.

Missing methodological details undermine reproducibility: key hyperparameters (DPO beta, update frequency f, dataset size |D|, learning rate, population size M, number of generations, tournament selection parameters) are described only qualitatively or not at all; the claimed 'anonymous repository' is not verifiable from the manuscript. GFlowNets are introduced in the preliminaries and claimed to be part of the hyperparameter sweep in Appendix A.3, yet no GFlowNet results appear in Table 1 or anywhere in the paper.

Statistical rigor is weak: no significance tests or confidence analysis are provided, and the std of the headline HV metric is large (e.g., 0.135 vs. 0.138/0.126 for ablations), so the margin over the sft_coevolve and rl_coevolve variants may not be meaningful despite the strong claims.

There is no limitations section, and several inconsistencies are left unaddressed: the prompt in Appendix A.1 says to 'decrease the DRD2 value' while Section 3/4 frames DRD2 as binding affinity to be maximized; the prompt and appendix contain errors ('GSK3β' written as 'GSK303b2', 'SIMLES', 'ZINK'). These raise concerns about carefulness of the experimental setup and objective definitions.

The contribution is incremental: combining an LLM as an evolutionary operator with periodic DPO fine-tuning of a small model is a natural extension of existing single-LLM evolutionary pipelines, and the delta over the strongest simple baseline (sft_coevolve) is modest on fitness metrics; the validity score of the full method (0.820) is actually the lowest among most variants.
Figures are of low quality and resolution (Figures 2-5), making it difficult to verify the claimed performance gaps, and Figure 3's qualitative narrative is not backed by quantitative evidence.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and clearly motivated: coupling a frozen closed-source LLM (global exploration) with a lightweight trainable local model that internalizes experience via DPO addresses a real gap in LLM-based evolutionary search, going beyond prompt engineering/RAG and beyond one-way distillation.

The similarity-filtered preference construction (global similarity filter F, stratified high/low pools, relaxed windows I1-I3 with fallback rules, Algorithm 2) is a concrete, well-specified technique, and the ablations (Table 2) plus the loss-stability comparison (Fig. 6) provide reasonable evidence that it improves DPO training stability.

Experimental breadth is good: comparisons against multiple training paradigms (SFT, RL) and SOTA baselines (REINVENT, MoLLEO, GFlowNet, DyMol), ablations over similarity strategy, API/local call split, and update frequency, orthogonal AutoDock Vina docking validation (Tables 3-4), extension to MOTSP/MOCVRP/Circle Packing, and a transparent cost analysis (Table 8).

Honest limitations section; the discussion of why explicit reward-based RL failed and why SFT caused catastrophic forgetting (Table 1 shows SFT's low uniqueness 0.478) adds useful empirical insight into training paradigms for LLM-driven molecular search.
weaknesses: Presentation defects suggest insufficient proofreading: Section 3.2.1 contains broken references ('Table ??' twice), the reference list cites several entries with implausible/inconsistent venues (e.g., 'Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 37' dated 2024 alongside many 2025 arXiv preprints), and the abstract sentence ends mid-sentence ('The code of MCCE is available on').

The central 'state-of-the-art Pareto front quality' claim is overstated: in Table 1, DyMol achieves clearly higher Hypervolume (0.871 vs. MCCE's 0.738) and higher AUC-Top10, and MCCE's validity (0.922) is notably below all molecular baselines (0.983-1.000). MCCE wins mainly on Top1/Top10 fitness, where margins over DyMol/GFN (4.35 vs. 4.23-4.24) are small relative to the reported std (up to ±0.25), and no statistical significance tests are reported.

Methodological novelty is modest: the framework is evolutionary LLM search plus DPO with a heuristic similarity filter; there is no theoretical analysis of why the similarity constraint stabilizes DPO, and the 'co-evolution' framing is weakened by the fact that the large model only changes via prompts while only the small model receives parameter updates.

Generalization evidence is thin: the combinatorial results (Table 5) show MCCE losing to AlphaEvolve on MOTSP, and Circle Packing gains over the record are marginal (2.635983 vs. 2.634+); per-task details (budgets, prompt formats, verifier implementations) for these domains are sparse.

Comparability concerns: baselines presumably reimplemented under a 5,000-candidate budget, but reimplementation details, hyperparameter sweeps per baseline, and how the hybrid selection strategy (Appendix A.9, which itself seems consequential for HV/uniqueness) interacts with baselines are not fully described; dependence on a proprietary GPT-4o API further limits reproducibility despite the code release claim.

Several claims lack direct support: the claim that the co-evolutionary collaboration 'outperforms the trajectory of either model alone' (Fig. 3) is based on qualitative curve inspection, and the DPO loss analysis (Fig. 4) shows peaks that the authors interpret favorably without quantitative comparison.

strengths: The paper systematically compares alternative training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO) within the same co-evolutionary framework, which is an informative ablation and motivates the DPO design choice.

The similarity-based data synthesis for DPO pair construction is a reasonable, clearly described heuristic for stabilizing preference learning when prompts have conflicting responses, supported by loss-curve comparisons (Figure 6).
The paper includes useful supplementary analyses: API cost/wall-clock accounting (Table 8), docking-based orthogonal validation (Table 4), and an SA-score analysis (Table 7).
Limitations are discussed honestly, and the framework is at least sketched generally enough (Appendix, Algorithm 2) that a motivated reader could attempt reproduction.
weaknesses: Central SOTA claims are not statistically supported. In Table 1, MCCE's Top-1 F (4.35 ± 0.17) overlaps heavily with GFlowNet (4.24 ± 0.25) and DyMol (4.23 ± 0.17); AUC-Top10 (4.02 ± 0.06) is actually worse than GFlowNet (4.08 ± 0.15) and DyMol (4.08 ± 0.05). No significance tests are reported, so 'consistently outperforms' is an overclaim.

The headline metrics conceal regressions: MCCE's Diversity (0.484) and Uniqueness (0.570) are markedly worse than most baselines (e.g., REINVENT 0.647 diversity; 0.98–1.00 uniqueness), which contradicts the narrative that co-evolution 'maintains diversity' and avoids premature convergence. Validity (0.820) is also below baselines.

Novelty is incremental. LLMs as evolutionary operators for molecular design (ExLLM, MoLLEO) and experience-driven fine-tuning are established; the contribution reduces to (a) alternating a frozen API model with a locally DPO-tuned model and (b) a heuristic similarity filter on preference pairs. The paper does not articulate why this is a fundamentally new learning problem or provide theoretical grounding for the co-evolution claim.

Presentation is unpolished for a main-track submission: broken cross-references ('Table ??' appears twice in Section 3.2.1), an incomplete sentence in the abstract ('The code of MCCE is available on'), low-resolution figures, and a main algorithm explicitly labeled 'simplified' with details deferred to the appendix.

Reproducibility is questionable: the method depends on a proprietary, frozen closed-source model (GPT-4o-2024-05-13) whose behavior can change, the code availability statement is truncated, and baseline comparisons do not establish equal LLM call budgets across methods, making the SOTA comparison potentially unfair.

Generalization evidence is thin and partly negative: on MOTSP, MCCE (1.025) underperforms AlphaEvolve (1.029 is better under minimization), and Circle Packing gains are marginal (2.635983 vs 2.634+). These results undermine the claim of a 'general-purpose' framework.
The docking validation (Section 3.3) is mixed: DRD2 and GSK3β docking scores actually worsen (−8.400 → −8.141 and −7.791 → −7.625), yet the text frames this positively; only JNK3 clearly improves.

The hyperparameter comparison in Appendix A.3 (Eq. 12) defines performance as a max over all explored configurations, which is a post-hoc selection procedure and an unsound basis for claiming one training paradigm is superior.

Several claims lack supporting evidence or detail: 'extensive hyperparameter sweeps' are asserted without a table of configurations, the DPO/TRL setup details (learning rate, β, LoRA vs full fine-tuning) are omitted, and the 'breakthrough' trajectory definition is informal.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and timely: pairing a frozen closed-source LLM (global exploration) with a lightweight trainable local model (experience internalization) via DPO addresses a real gap in LLM-based evolutionary search, where prior systems (ExLLM, MoLLEO) rely on a single frozen model that cannot accumulate experience.

The paper does not just propose the final method but systematically diagnoses why SFT (catastrophic forgetting/memorization) and RL (instability with sparse, uninterpretable rewards) fail in this setting. This ablation over training paradigms is a genuine contribution and strengthens the motivation for the DPO design.

The similarity-based data synthesis pipeline is well specified: global similarity statistics, a similarity filter, nested relaxation windows, and explicit fallback rules are all described (Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2), which supports reproducibility.

Evaluation goes beyond benchmark property scores: AutoDock Vina docking validation (Section 3.3) provides an orthogonal check against proxy-oracle exploitation, the SA analysis (Table 7) shows generated molecules remain synthetically accessible, and a cost analysis (Table 8) makes resource requirements transparent.

Results on three additional combinatorial problems (Circle Packing with a new record on n=31, MOTSP, MOCVRP) plus the ablations over similarity strategy, API/local split, and update frequency (Table 2) support the claimed generality of the framework.
An honest limitations section acknowledges the molecular-centric validation, domain-specific similarity metrics, and unexplored continuous/mixed-variable settings.
weaknesses: The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim is not cleanly supported by the evidence. In Table 1, GFNNet achieves the best HV (0.871 vs. 0.855) and DyMoL matches Top1F (4.24), while MCCE's Top1F advantage (4.35 vs. 4.24) has overlapping standard deviations (±0.17 vs. ±0.25) with only 5 runs. No statistical significance testing is reported for any comparison, yet improvements of 0.1 on a 4-point fitness scale are small.

Compute-budget fairness is a concern: MCCE uses both GPT-4o API calls and a 7B local model fine-tuned on 8×A800 GPUs, whereas baselines like GFNNet and DyMoL are single-model methods. The paper does not report or equalize the total compute/API budget across methods, so 'better performance under a fixed budget' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Generalization evidence is mixed: on MOTSP, MCCE (1.025206) is worse than AlphaEvolve (1.029279); only MOCVRP is won. Claiming broad extensibility from one of three combinatorial wins overstates the result.

The similarity-based data synthesis is a heuristic with no theoretical or empirical isolation of which component matters most. The claim that it 'reduces distribution shift' is argued qualitatively; Figure 6 shows loss stability but there is no direct measurement of distribution shift or of why structural comparability of pairs is the operative factor.

Several technical details needed for reproducibility are under-specified in the main text: the local fine-tuning procedure (LoRA vs. full fine-tuning, learning rate, DPO β), how the scalar ranking score for stratification is computed from the multi-objective vector, and the exact effect of population-dependent score normalization (Eq. 5) on reported metrics.

Presentation issues: a broken cross-reference ('Table ??' in Section 3.2.1), relatively high variance in several ablation rows (e.g., HV 0.855±0.128 vs. 0.770±0.388) that weakens the ablation conclusions, and dependence on a closed-source API model (GPT-4o-2024-05-13) that limits full reproducibility even with released code.

Novelty is moderate: the framework is a combination of known ingredients — LLM-as-evolutionary-operator search (ExLLM, MoLLEO, ReEVO), DPO preference learning, and similarity filtering — with the main new element being the similarity-windowed preference pair construction. This is a useful but incremental contribution relative to the related-work landscape the paper itself surveys (Wu et al. 2025b, Yu et al. 2025).
